paper.title_en: StAGE: Stellar Archaeology-driven Galaxy Evolution II. Binary Black Hole Mergers in Quiescent Galaxies and their Star-forming Progenitors
paper.abstract_en: We apply StAGE, a data-driven galaxy-evolution framework based on stellar archaeology, to study binary black hole (BBH) mergers associated with present-day quiescent galaxies (QGs) and their star-forming progenitors. By combining StAGE star-formation and chemical-enrichment histories with pre-computed SEVN population-synthesis catalogs, we predict the BBH merger-rate density, intrinsic binary properties, merger-time host-galaxy distributions, and the associated stochastic gravitational-wave (GW) background. A distinctive feature of StAGE is that it jointly tracks the stellar-binary environment at birth and the properties of the host galaxy at merger time. Moreover, stellar-archaeology constraints on $α$-enhancement allow us to explore how adopting the iron abundance relevant for massive-star winds, rather than oxygen-based total metallicity, affects the predicted BBH merger rates. We find that most BBHs form at moderately subsolar metallicities $Z\lesssim Z_\odot/3$, while their merger-time hosts typically have stellar masses $M_\star\sim10^{10}-10^{11.5}\,M_\odot$ at $z\lesssim2$. At and beyond cosmic noon, hosts lie mainly on the star-forming main sequence, whereas starbursting and quenching descendants contribute increasingly toward lower redshift. Using the independent approach offered by StAGE, we also confirm recent literature findings that, for most binary-evolution prescriptions, predicted local BBH merger rates exceed the LVK-inferred range, while dynamical formation in stellar clusters extends the BBH primary mass distribution into the high-mass regime poorly populated by isolated binaries. Finally, the predicted stochastic background approaches the projected sensitivity of planned LVK upgrades and lies within reach of the Einstein Telescope. All in all, StAGE can provide physically motivated host priors for GW-source localization and dark-siren cosmology.
